articles.title: Architecture and the Architect Role: Software, Solution, Enterprise and Cloud Architects
articles.scope: Defines software architecture (structures, building blocks, decisions) and separates it from design. Contrasts software, solution, enterprise, cloud, security, data and AI-solution architects by scope, time horizon, deliverables and stakeholders. Covers the goals, benefits and long-term impact of architecture, the architect's tasks and skills, and how architects work with product owners, developers, operations and executives. Afterwards the reader can place any architecture task at the right level and say which role owns it.

articles.title: Stakeholders, Requirements, Constraints and Assumptions
articles.scope: Shows how to identify stakeholders and their concerns, and how to resolve conflicts between short-term business goals and long-term architecture goals (CPSA-F LG 02-01, R1). Separates functional requirements, quality requirements, constraints and assumptions. A constraint table follows LG 02-02: technological constraints such as reference architectures, libraries and frameworks (R1); organisational ones such as team structure, budget, staff and skills (R1), and Conway's law, standards and process models (R2); regulatory ones (R2); and trends such as cloud and generative AI (R3). Covers making assumptions explicit (LG 02-05), validating requirements, and turning business goals into measurable, architecturally significant requirements. Afterwards the reader can produce a stakeholder table, a categorised constraint list, an assumption log and a prioritised ASR list.

articles.title: Quality Attributes, Quality Models and Quality Scenarios
articles.scope: Explains qualities as system properties that interact and trade off, using three reference models: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, the arc42 quality model Q42 (nine top-level qualities used as flat tags), and ISO/IEC 25059 for AI systems. The AI coverage adds qualities such as groundedness, safety, nondeterminism and cost per task, linked to ai/evaluation-ops. Teaches the iSAQB four-part scenario (context, stimulus, response, measurement) and the method of analysis each requirement must name (LG 02-04, R1), and maps it to the SEI six-part form; utility trees and quality attribute workshops are labelled as SEI extensions. Warns that a metric used as a target can stop measuring what matters (R2; Goodhart's law, R3), and links targets to SLOs in devops/sre. Afterwards the reader can write testable scenarios and rank them by business value and technical risk.

articles.title: Design Approaches Compared: Top-Down, Bottom-Up, View-Based, Domain-Driven, Evolutionary and Risk-Driven
articles.scope: Compares the approaches CPSA-F LG 03-03 names. Top-down and bottom-up design and view-based development are rated R1. Domain-driven design, evolutionary architecture, global analysis and model-based design are rated R3; DDD and the patterns themselves are linked to architecture/patterns. Adds widely used approaches outside the curriculum, labelled as such: Attribute-Driven Design, risk-driven 'just enough' architecture, big design up front versus emergent design, the last responsible moment, one-way and two-way door decisions, spikes and architectural runway. Explains how iteration and feedback loops reduce risk (LG 03-05). Afterwards the reader can choose and justify a design approach for a given risk profile and team structure.

articles.title: From Drivers to Structure: Solution Strategy, Decomposition and Building-Block Design
articles.scope: A worked how-to for the R1 core of CPSA-F chapter 3. It covers driving design from the qualities to be achieved (LG 03-01), writing the solution strategy (arc42 section 4), and decomposing a system hierarchically with black-box and white-box descriptions and stepwise refinement (LG 03-02). Covers deciding which dependencies are justified, static versus dynamic and afferent versus efferent coupling (LG 03-06), separating domain from technical building blocks, and tracing decisions to code. C# samples show .NET project boundaries and internal visibility; Python samples show package boundaries. Principles and patterns are linked to architecture/patterns. Afterwards the reader can turn a set of drivers into a solution strategy and a first building-block view.

articles.title: Socio-technical Architecture: Conway's Law, Team Topologies and Cognitive Load
articles.scope: Explains Conway's law, which CPSA-F LG 02-02 rates as an R2 organisational constraint, and the inverse Conway manoeuvre. Introduces Team Topologies' four team types and three interaction modes, and team cognitive load. Maps platform teams and workload teams onto the CAF and Azure Well-Architected roles that cloud-operating-models uses. Contrasts organising teams by component, feature and stream, and shows how team boundaries made decompositions succeed or fail. Afterwards the reader can test a proposed decomposition against team boundaries and propose team changes that make the target architecture achievable.

articles.title: Architecture Analysis and Evaluation: Scenario-Based Reviews, Metrics, ATAM and Lightweight Methods
articles.scope: Starts with the reasons for analysis in LG 05-01 (R1): finding risks, checking that requirements are met, checking conformance and confirming that stakeholder concerns are addressed. Then teaches the LG 05-02 R1 methods: acceptance-test analysis, runtime measurement, qualitative evaluation (interviews, surveys, penetration tests), scenario-based analysis and coupling metrics. Their evidence sources include source-code metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, test results, error clusters and runtime logs. Compares ATAM and CBAM (both R3), ARID, risk storming, weighted decision matrices and Well-Architected reviews by cost, depth and timing, using risks, non-risks, risk themes, sensitivity points and trade-off points. Afterwards the reader can choose an evaluation method, run a lightweight scenario-based review and turn its findings into ADRs and backlog items.

articles.title: Architecture Decision Records: Nygard, MADR 4 and Y-Statements
articles.scope: Covers making, justifying and documenting architectural decisions and the dependencies between them (CPSA-F LG 04-08, R1), then the ADR format itself (R2). Explains which decisions deserve a record and compares the Nygard, MADR 4.0.0 and Y-statement templates. Explains the status lifecycle (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded), links between superseding decisions, and storing decision logs as docs-as-code with pull-request review. It also defines the template this library's decisions/ folder uses. Afterwards the reader can set up an ADR log in a repository and write a decision with drivers, options, consequences and confirmation.

articles.title: Build, Buy or Extend: Technology Selection, Vendor Evaluation and Lock-in
articles.scope: Compares building, buying (SaaS, packaged or managed services) and extending an existing platform. The criteria are differentiation, time to value, TCO, skills, operability, compliance and exit cost. Teaches weighted decision matrices, proofs of concept, technology radars, vendor due diligence and lock-in scoring, with each outcome recorded as an ADR. Applies the method to four cases: SAP-C02's adoption of managed services and new technologies, CAF's replace versus rebuild choice, TOGAF Phase E solution selection, and AB-100's decision to build, buy or extend AI components (for example custom agents versus extending Microsoft 365 Copilot). Afterwards the reader can run a defensible selection and state the exit cost of the chosen option.

articles.title: Architecture Principles and Standards: Writing, Applying and Retiring Them
articles.scope: Teaches the TOGAF Architecture Principles technique (name, statement, rationale, implications) and when principles are set, in the Preliminary phase and Phase A. Separates principles from standards, guidelines and constraints. Contrasts enterprise principles with Well-Architected design principles, the FinOps principles, Zero Trust principles (linked to security/foundations) and code-level design principles (linked to architecture/patterns). Covers testing a principle set for conflicts, applying it in reviews and ADRs, turning standards into guardrails and retiring outdated rules. Afterwards the reader can write a small, testable principle set and a standards catalogue.

articles.title: The C4 Model: Context, Container, Component and Code Diagrams
articles.scope: Explains the C4 abstractions, the four core and three supplementary diagram types, the notation rules (titles, keys, technology labels) and common mistakes, such as confusing a C4 container with a Docker container. Notes that CPSA-F rates C4 R3 (LG 04-03 and 04-09), and shows how C4 diagrams realise the R1 context, building-block and deployment views of LG 04-05. Contrasts C4 with UML and ArchiMate, and shows diagrams-as-code with Structurizr DSL, Mermaid and PlantUML. Afterwards the reader can draw consistent context, container and deployment diagrams for a system that runs on both clouds.

articles.title: UML for Architecture Description: Class, Package, Component, Deployment, Sequence and Activity Diagrams
articles.scope: Covers the UML diagrams CPSA-F LG 04-03 rates R2 (class, package, component, deployment, sequence and activity) and those it rates R3 (composite structure and state machine), limited to the notation an architect actually needs. Shows which diagram serves which view (building block, runtime, deployment). Contrasts UML with C4, ArchiMate, BPMN, entity-relationship diagrams and numbered step lists. Includes diagrams-as-code in PlantUML and Mermaid. Afterwards the reader can read and draw the UML diagrams the exam expects and choose the lightest notation that answers a stakeholder's concern.

articles.title: Views, Viewpoints and Architecture Description: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, 4+1, Rozanski-Woods and arc42
articles.scope: Puts the R1 content first: the context, building-block, runtime and deployment views of CPSA-F LG 04-05, view-based development (LG 03-03), and the black-box and white-box levels. Then defines architecture description, concerns, viewpoints, views and model kinds as ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 uses them (R3). Compares Kruchten's 4+1 view model, Rozanski and Woods' viewpoints and perspectives, the arc42 views and TOGAF/ArchiMate viewpoints. Clarifies view versus viewpoint and how to choose a minimal set of views per stakeholder. Afterwards the reader can design the view set for an architecture description and justify each view by the concerns it answers.

articles.title: Documenting and Communicating Architecture: arc42, Docs-as-Code and Audience-Specific Communication
articles.scope: Covers CPSA-F's R1 documentation goals: quality criteria and audience fit (LG 04-01), consistent communication with templates for different audiences (LG 04-02), and documenting internal and external interfaces (LG 04-06). Also covers documenting cross-cutting concepts (LG 04-07, R2). Walks through the twelve arc42 sections (R3) and how to tailor them, and keeps documentation current with docs-as-code and diagrams-as-code built in CI. Covers audience-specific formats (executive one-pagers, design reviews, RFCs, the architect elevator) and documentation anti-patterns. Afterwards the reader can set up an arc42 skeleton, document an interface properly and produce material for each stakeholder group from a single source.

articles.title: Evolutionary Architecture and Fitness Functions
articles.scope: Explains evolutionary architecture, an R3 approach in CPSA-F LG 03-03: guided incremental change, appropriate coupling and reversibility. Covers the fitness-function taxonomy: atomic or holistic, triggered or continual, static or dynamic. Implements dependency-rule checks with ArchUnitNET or NetArchTest in C# and import-linter or PyTestArch in Python, then adds latency and cost fitness functions in CI. Relates these checks to architecture conformance (LG 05-03, R2) and to catching erosion early. Afterwards the reader can add automated architecture conformance checks to a pipeline.

articles.title: Technical Debt, Architecture Erosion and Drift
articles.scope: Defines technical debt (principal and interest), Fowler's technical debt quadrant and architectural debt, and contrasts debt with erosion and drift. Covers making debt visible in a debt register and arc42 section 11, using error clusters and change rates as evidence, and estimating interest. Covers paying debt down through refactoring, strangler-style replacement or the choice of migration strategy, including the CAF observation that rehosting carries existing debt into the cloud. Afterwards the reader can maintain a prioritised debt register and argue for remediation in business terms.

articles.title: Architecture Governance Models: Review Boards, TOGAF Architecture Boards, Advice Process and Guardrails
articles.scope: Compares governance models by speed, consistency and accountability. Covers centralised review boards and the TOGAF Architecture Board (compliance reviews, Architecture Contracts, dispensations), federated design authorities, the advice process with ADRs, and automated guardrails such as policy-as-code and fitness functions. A dedicated section relates architecture governance to cloud resource governance. For AZ-305 that means management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, tagging and Azure Policy; for SAP-C02 Task 1.4 it means a multi-account governance model with AWS Organizations, SCPs and Control Tower. Both link to the provider governance pages. Afterwards the reader can design a governance model that fits an organisation's size, risk appetite and delivery cadence, and say which controls belong to architecture governance and which to platform policy.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Architecture Practice: Review, Migration and Documentation Agents and Their Limits
articles.scope: Surveys agentic tools that now do architecture work. The AWS Well-Architected Agent (preview) ranks recommendations against business goals, proposes IaC fixes and reviews CDK or Terraform projects on demand. The Azure Copilot migration agent (preview) supports migration planning, and AWS Transform runs agentic migration jobs with human approvals. LLM assistants draft ADRs, C4 diagrams and arc42 sections. Sets out the controls for responsible use: evaluating output quality, approval gates, provenance and audit trails, accountability for decisions, and data-exposure and prompt-injection risk, with links to ai/agents, ai/evaluation-ops and security/ai-security. Afterwards the reader can decide which architecture tasks to delegate to an agent and design the review controls around them.

articles.title: Case Study: Describing a Real-Time Market-Data Platform with arc42, C4 and ADRs
articles.scope: Documents one complete example system, modelled on the .NET, Angular, Redis Streams and TimescaleDB stack used in this library's messaging/, data/ and frontend/ sections. It starts from quality goals, constraints and context and works through the solution strategy, the building-block, runtime and deployment views, cross-cutting concepts, ADRs, quality scenarios, and risks and technical debt. It serves as the worked 'example of a software architecture' that CPSA-F chapter 6 asks candidates to know (not examined), and shows how the practice articles fit together. Afterwards the reader can use it as a model when documenting their own systems.

articles.title: Well-Architected Frameworks: Anatomy, Purpose and Limits
articles.scope: Explains what a Well-Architected framework contains: pillars, design principles, questions or checklists, best practices, documented trade-offs, lenses or workload guidance, maturity guidance and review tooling. Shows how it differs from a Cloud Adoption Framework and from reference architectures. Compares the pillar sets at a glance: Azure has five, AWS has six (including sustainability), and Microsoft Power Platform Well-Architected has five, including Experience Optimization and with no Cost Optimization pillar. Mentions the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework and links to cloud/compare for the full Azure-vs-AWS mapping. Afterwards the reader can explain where a WAF fits in the architecture lifecycle and which framework and artefact to use when.

articles.title: Azure Well-Architected Framework: Pillars, Checklists, Maturity Model and Workload Guidance
articles.scope: Goes pillar by pillar through Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence and Performance Efficiency. For each pillar it covers design principles, design review checklists, key design strategies, tradeoffs and risks, the design patterns mapped to it, and the five-level maturity model with its assessment. Then covers the layers above the pillars: workload guidance (for example AI, SaaS, mission-critical, HPC, sustainability, Microsoft Fabric), service guides, design guides, the Architect's fundamentals and checklist pages, guidance on adopting AI in operations, the Azure Well-Architected Review, and how Azure Advisor maps to the pillars. Relates the framework to the AZ-305 design objectives and to SC-100's CAF- and WAF-based security and governance strategy. Afterwards the reader can apply WAF checklists and maturity levels to an Azure design.

articles.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework: Six Pillars, Design Principles and Lenses
articles.scope: Covers the framework's definitions (component, workload, architecture, milestone, technology portfolio, level of effort), its general design principles, the six pillars with their question and best-practice structure, and the current revision dated 6 November 2024. Describes the Lens Catalog in the Well-Architected Tool, lens whitepapers (for example Serverless Applications, SaaS, Generative AI, Machine Learning, Agentic AI, Financial Services Industry) and custom lenses. Shows how SAA-C03's four domains and SAP-C02's tasks map onto the pillars. Afterwards the reader can navigate the pillar questions and choose the lenses an exam scenario implies.

articles.title: Pillar Trade-offs: Reliability, Security, Cost, Performance, Operations and Sustainability in Tension
articles.scope: Analyses recurring tensions (reliability vs cost, performance vs cost, security vs operability, sustainability vs redundancy, user experience vs control), with worked Azure and AWS examples. Shows how each framework documents trade-offs. Azure publishes per-pillar tradeoff pages and flags tradeoffs and risks in its guidance. AWS states that security and operational excellence are generally not traded off. The AWS Well-Architected Agent reports cross-pillar impacts and trade-offs for each recommendation across its four optimisation pillars, one of which it calls 'resilience'. Shows how to record trade-offs as ADRs and relate them to ATAM sensitivity and trade-off points. Afterwards the reader can defend a design that deliberately under-invests in one pillar for a stated business reason.

articles.title: Running a Well-Architected Review: Scoping, Facilitation, Risks and Improvement Plans
articles.scope: Follows AWS's documented Well-Architected Framework Review: prepare (workload and scope, people and culture, documentation and infrastructure), run, then improve (identify and understand risks, determine prescriptive solutions, prioritise, implement and track). Applies the same flow on Azure. Provider tabs cover the AWS Well-Architected Tool (lenses, custom lenses, review templates, profiles, milestones and milestone reports, dashboard, Trusted Advisor, AppRegistry and Jira integrations, EventBridge, API) and, for Azure, the Well-Architected Review and maturity-model assessments with Azure Advisor. A tooling section covers the AWS Well-Architected Agent (preview): weekly goal-ranked recommendations with IaC fixes, on-demand IaC reviews and its support-plan prerequisite. C# and Python samples move open high- and medium-risk issues from the WA Tool API into a backlog. Afterwards the reader can run a review end to end and track remediation.

articles.title: Sustainable Architecture: The AWS Sustainability Pillar, Azure Sustainable Workloads and Carbon Measurement
articles.scope: Treats sustainability as an architecture quality and explains why it is a pillar on AWS but workload guidance on Azure. Covers the AWS sustainability pillar's design principles and the Azure Well-Architected sustainability workload guidance. Teaches measurement and reduction: Software Carbon Intensity (ISO/IEC 21031), greenhouse-gas emissions scopes, carbon-aware scheduling, utilisation and rightsizing. Shows the overlap with cost optimisation and with the FinOps Sustainability capability. Provider carbon-reporting tools are linked from cloud/azure/cost and cloud/aws/cost. Afterwards the reader can set a sustainability objective for a workload and choose design changes that reduce its footprint.

articles.title: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure, Manage
articles.scope: Explains the CAF's seven phases and the decision each answers. Strategy has four steps: define motivations, mission and objectives; define the strategy team; prepare the organisation (executive buy-in, operating-model readiness, the shift from project to product); and inform the strategy on cost efficiency, resiliency, security and sustainability. Covers the Plan steps, Ready with Azure landing zones, Adopt (the five migration steps: plan, prepare workloads, execute, optimize, decommission; plus modernize and cloud-native), and Govern, Secure and Manage. Covers the AI adoption (with an AI Center of Excellence), AI agents, data platform, sovereignty and Azure VMware Solution scenarios. Maps the matching CAF objectives in AZ-305, SC-100 and AB-100. Afterwards the reader can structure an Azure adoption plan and know which CAF guidance answers which decision.

articles.title: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework: Perspectives, Capabilities and the Transformation Journey
articles.scope: Covers the six AWS CAF perspectives and their foundational capabilities, the four transformation domains (technology, process, organization, product) and the Envision, Align, Launch and Scale journey. Adds the AWS CAF for AI whitepaper, which extends them to AI, ML and generative AI adoption. Connects the CAF to the Migration Acceleration Program: Assess produces a readiness assessment across the CAF dimensions and a TCO model (linked to tco-and-cloud-business-case), Mobilize closes the gaps and builds the operational foundation, and Migrate & Modernize executes. Also covers MAP's variants for Microsoft, VMware, SAP and mainframe workloads. Afterwards the reader can run a readiness gap analysis by perspective and turn it into a migration programme plan.

articles.title: Cloud Operating Models: Centralized, Shared Management and Decentralized
articles.scope: Compares centralized, shared-management (platform plus workload teams) and decentralized cloud operating models and their hybrids by control, speed, risk and fit. Covers the roles involved (cloud strategy team, cloud center of excellence, platform team, workload teams, governance and security teams) and the move from project to product funding. Relates each model to landing-zone ownership, multi-subscription and multi-account governance, and central FinOps enablement, and links to socio-technical-architecture for team design. Afterwards the reader can recommend an operating model and a responsibility matrix for an organisation.

articles.title: Migration Strategies from Retire to Rebuild: The AWS 7 Rs, Microsoft CAF Strategies and Gartner TIME
articles.scope: Defines retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase or replace, refactor, rearchitect and rebuild as provider-neutral treatments. Notes that CAF's like-for-like rehost also covers PaaS to PaaS moves (for example AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Azure App Service), and that the frameworks mean different things by 'refactor'. A mapping table links AWS's 7 Rs to CAF's eight strategies; the Rosetta pair itself lives in cloud/compare. Relates both to Gartner's TIME model. Gives decision criteria, success metrics per strategy, and anti-patterns such as rehosting problem workloads or refactoring during a large migration. Relocate is developed in vmware-estate-migration. Afterwards the reader can assign and justify a strategy for each workload in AZ-305 and SAP-C02 scenarios.

articles.title: Portfolio Discovery and Assessment: Inventory, Dependencies, Readiness and Right-Sizing
articles.scope: Shows how to build a migration inventory (agentless appliance, agents, collector or CMDB import), map direct, indirect and business dependencies, assess readiness, right-size (performance-based or as-is), evaluate TCO and score workloads by business value, complexity and risk. Follows SAP-C02 Task 4.1 and AZ-305's 'evaluate on-premises servers, data, and applications for migration'. Provider tabs cover Azure Migrate (new and classic experiences, appliance, collector, assessments, business case, the Azure Copilot migration agent in preview), and AWS Transform discovery and assessment plus Migration Evaluator. A table maps exam-guide names to current ones: AWS Migration Hub and AWS Application Discovery Service closed to new customers on 7 November 2025 in favour of AWS Transform, and AWS Application Migration Service is now AWS Transform MGN. Afterwards the reader can produce an assessed portfolio that feeds strategy selection and wave planning.

articles.title: Migration Readiness and Security: Landing Zones, Hybrid Connectivity, Identity, DNS and Securing Migration Tooling
articles.scope: Covers what must be ready before the first wave: a landing zone and governance model (AWS Organizations and Control Tower, Azure landing zones), team skills and external support, and hybrid connectivity. It also covers the data path (Direct Connect or ExpressRoute, site-to-site VPN, shipped devices or public internet, as CAF compares them), identity (IAM Identity Center and Directory Service, Microsoft Entra ID and AD DS) and DNS cutover with Route 53 or Azure DNS. Teaches SAP-C02 Task 4.2's 'applying the appropriate security methods to migration tools': least-privilege roles for discovery and replication tools, appliance credential handling, encrypted and private replication traffic, protected staging data and logs, and secure decommissioning. Links the provider networking, identity and governance pages and SC-100's landing-zone security objective. Afterwards the reader can produce a migration readiness checklist and a security design for the migration tooling.

articles.title: Wave Planning, Migration Factories and Cutover
articles.scope: Teaches grouping servers into move groups and waves by direct, indirect and business dependencies, risk and the business calendar. Plan only the next wave in detail, migrate pilot and non-production waves first, and manage split-environment operation for components that cannot move yet. Covers scaling through a migration factory (roles, runbooks, automation, metrics), review checkpoints at 25%, 50% and 75% of each wave, and choosing downtime or near-zero-downtime migration per workload. Also covers rollback criteria and tested rollback plans, go/no-go decisions, hypercare and decommissioning, following CAF's migrate steps. Provider tabs cover AWS Transform wave planning, AWS Transform MGN applications and waves, and Azure Migrate migration execution. Afterwards the reader can draft a wave plan and a cutover runbook with rollback gates.

articles.title: Data and Database Migration: Online vs Offline, Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
articles.scope: Compares online migration (replication and CDC; CAF calls it near-zero downtime) with offline (downtime) migration, and homogeneous with heterogeneous database moves that need schema and code conversion. Also compares network and device-based bulk transfer, including CAF's data-path choice (ExpressRoute, VPN, Data Box, public internet). Includes transfer-time and cost calculators in C# and Python. Provider tabs cover, for Azure: Azure Database Migration Service (SQL Server to Azure SQL Database offline only; to SQL Managed Instance or SQL Server on Azure VMs online or offline), SSMA, AzCopy, Azure Storage Mover, Azure File Sync and Data Box. For AWS they cover DMS with DMS Schema Conversion and AWS SCT, DataSync, Transfer Family, S3 Transfer Acceleration and Data Transfer Terminal. A note explains that the AWS Snow Family devices named in SAP-C02 are no longer available to new customers. Afterwards the reader can choose transfer mechanisms that meet downtime, security and timeline constraints.

articles.title: Choosing Target Platforms for Migrated Workloads: IaaS, PaaS, Containers or Serverless
articles.scope: A provider-neutral decision framework for SAP-C02 Task 4.3 ('Determine a new architecture for existing workloads') and AZ-305's 'recommend a solution for migrating workloads to IaaS and PaaS'. Choose the compute, container-hosting, storage and database targets by compatibility, operational burden, licensing, scaling and cost. Works through typical .NET, Java and SQL Server estates. Examples: SQL Server to a VM, a managed instance or a cloud-native database; IIS applications to VMs, App Service, Elastic Beanstalk or containers. Provider tabs link to the compute and storage-data folders and to cloud/compare. Afterwards the reader can recommend and justify a target platform for each workload in a migration scenario.

articles.title: VMware Estate Migration: Relocate vs Rehost vs Replatform
articles.scope: Compares three exits from an on-premises VMware estate. Relocate moves the hypervisor stack to a cloud-hosted VMware platform: Azure VMware Solution, or Amazon Elastic VMware Service, which runs VMware Cloud Foundation inside your VPC. Rehost converts VMs to native cloud VMs with Azure Migrate, AWS Transform for VMware or AWS Transform MGN. Replatform moves workloads onto PaaS or containers. Weighs licensing and subscription changes, timeline, skills, networking (layer-2 extension, IP retention), operations and cost. Places relocate in the AWS 7 Rs, notes that CAF lists no such strategy and handles VMware through its Azure VMware Solution scenario instead, and links MAP for VMware workloads. Afterwards the reader can recommend a VMware exit path and its sequencing.

articles.title: Modernization Pathways: Migrate-Then-Modernize, Containerize, Re-architect or Replace
articles.scope: Describes when to modernize during migration and when to wait until afterwards. Covers the main pathways and their prerequisites and risks: managed and purpose-built databases, containerization, serverless and event-driven decomposition, strangler-fig replacement of monoliths, SaaS replacement, and .NET Framework and mainframe modernization, including agentic tooling such as AWS Transform. Draws on SAP-C02 Task 4.4 ('Determine opportunities for modernization and enhancements') and CAF modernize guidance, and links to architecture/patterns and the messaging articles for target designs. Afterwards the reader can propose a staged modernization roadmap for a migrated workload.

articles.title: Cloud Exit, Repatriation and Reversibility
articles.scope: Covers the reverse journey: why organisations leave a provider or service (cost, regulation, concentration risk, performance, sovereignty), and the CCSP concepts of portability, interoperability, reversibility and vendor lock-in. Teaches designing and testing an exit plan, covering triggers, target options, data export formats and egress cost, contract terms on termination and data deletion, escrow and timelines. Covers regulatory exit-strategy requirements such as those in the EU's DORA for critical ICT services, and the multicloud and abstraction trade-offs that reduce lock-in at a price. Links security/grc for contracts and third-party risk and cloud/foundations for multicloud. Afterwards the reader can write an exit strategy for a critical workload and estimate its cost and duration.

articles.title: FinOps Fundamentals: Principles, Personas, Lifecycle, Maturity, Scopes and Domains
articles.scope: Introduces FinOps as the FinOps Foundation defines it, covering cloud and other technology: the six principles, core and allied personas, the Inform–Optimize–Operate lifecycle, Crawl–Walk–Run maturity, Scopes and technology categories, and the four domains with their capabilities. A table shows capability names before and after the 2026 update (for example Workload Optimization becomes Usage Optimization, and Policy & Governance becomes Governance, Policy & Risk) and the new Executive Strategy Alignment capability; it must be verified against finops.org before publication. Contrasts FinOps with cloud cost management, the WAF cost pillars, ITFM/TBM and ITAM. Afterwards the reader can explain the framework's structure and vocabulary at FinOps Certified Practitioner depth.

articles.title: Understanding Usage and Cost: Billing Data, FOCUS, Reporting and Anomaly Management
articles.scope: Explains how billing data is produced and ingested, and the FOCUS specification (v1.4, June 2026): its datasets and key columns (BilledCost, EffectiveCost, ListCost, ContractedCost, charge categories, commitment discount columns) and what each cost measure is for. Shows how to build reports, granular cost-and-usage investigations and anomaly detection on top of it. C# and Python samples load FOCUS exports from both clouds and compute amortized cost by service and owner. Provider tabs cover Microsoft Cost Management exports (FOCUS) and AWS Data Exports (FOCUS and CUR 2.0). Afterwards the reader can build a provider-neutral cost dataset and an anomaly alert.

articles.title: Cost Allocation: Tagging, Hierarchies, Shared Costs, Showback and Chargeback
articles.scope: Compares allocation mechanisms (account and subscription hierarchies, tags and labels, cost categories and allocation rules) and methods for splitting shared costs (even, proportional, fixed). Then contrasts showback with chargeback and their organisational effects. Covers tag governance and enforcement, untaggable spend, and allocation for Kubernetes and multi-tenant systems, with provider tabs and a C#/Python proportional-split example. Afterwards the reader can design a tagging strategy that maps costs to business units (SAP-C02 Task 1.5) and a resource-tagging strategy for AZ-305.

articles.title: Unit Economics, Forecasting and Budgeting: Quantifying Business Value
articles.scope: Teaches how to choose unit metrics (cost per customer, transaction, tenant, inference or agent task), separate fixed, variable and marginal cost, and define KPIs and benchmarks. Shows how to translate business requirements into measurable metrics and report cost avoidance separately from cost savings. Covers estimating with pricing calculators, trend-based and driver-based forecasting, and budgeting with variance analysis; budget alerts and enforcement are covered in cost-guardrails. C# and Python samples join FOCUS EffectiveCost to business telemetry. Afterwards the reader can publish a unit-cost dashboard and a driver-based forecast.

articles.title: Commitment Discounts and Rate Optimization: Reservations, Savings Plans, Spot and Negotiated Pricing
articles.scope: Explains usage-based commitments (reservations), spend-based commitments (savings plans), spot capacity, negotiated spend commitments and licensing levers. Covers the metrics that govern them: coverage, utilization, effective savings rate and break-even point. Contrasts discount commitments with capacity reservations, which guarantee capacity without a discount. Covers purchasing strategies (laddering, central purchasing, scope and sharing, trade-ins) and their risks. Provider tabs compare Azure reservations and the savings plans for compute and for databases with AWS Reserved Instances and the Compute, EC2 Instance, Database and SageMaker AI Savings Plans, including which database services each database plan covers. Afterwards the reader can size a commitment portfolio and explain how purchasing options affect cost and flexibility.

articles.title: Usage Optimization: Rightsizing, Scheduling, Idle-Resource Cleanup and the Optimization Loop
articles.scope: An operational how-to for the FinOps Usage Optimization capability and for these SAP-C02 skills: analysing usage reports for under- and over-utilised resources, finding unused resources, and designing a rightsizing strategy. Covers the optimisation loop (detect, decide, act, verify); rightsizing compute, databases and storage; scheduling non-production environments; removing idle and orphaned resources; autoscaling and storage lifecycle policies; and why usage work should precede commitment purchases. Provider tabs link Azure Advisor and Microsoft Cost Management, and AWS Compute Optimizer, Cost Optimization Hub and Trusted Advisor. C# and Python samples turn recommendations into tickets. Afterwards the reader can run a recurring usage-optimisation cycle with measurable savings.

articles.title: Data Transfer Cost Modelling: Zones, Regions, Internet Egress, NAT and Private Connectivity
articles.scope: Builds a provider-neutral model of data-transfer charges by path and direction. The paths are within and between availability zones, between regions, to and from the internet, through NAT gateways, load balancers and private endpoints, over VPN or dedicated circuits, and through CDNs. Applies SAP-C02 Task 2.6's 'Performing data transfer modeling and selecting services to reduce data transfer costs' with C# and Python calculators and Azure and AWS tabs. Shows design moves such as zone-affine routing, caching, compression, private connectivity and data locality. Afterwards the reader can estimate the transfer bill of an architecture before building it and reduce it with targeted design changes.

articles.title: Licensing and SaaS Cost Management: BYOL, License Mobility, Hybrid Benefit and SaaS Spend
articles.scope: Covers the FinOps Licensing & SaaS capability. Compares bring-your-own-licence with licence-included pricing and explains licence-mobility rules. Covers Windows Server and SQL Server licensing on Azure (Azure Hybrid Benefit) and on AWS (licence-included, or BYOL on dedicated hosts), and how licensing drives migration TCO and target-platform choice. Extends to SaaS spend: inventory, seat utilisation, renewals and shadow IT, with the link to IT asset management. Provider mechanics, the AWS Optimization and Licensing Assessment and MAP for Microsoft workloads are linked from the provider pages. Afterwards the reader can build a licensing position for a migration business case and a SaaS optimisation backlog.

articles.title: Cost Guardrails: Budgets, Alerts, Quotas, Policies and Automated Spend Controls
articles.scope: Brings preventive and detective cost controls together. These include budgets and threshold alerts, billing alarms based on expected usage patterns, anomaly alerts, quotas and rate limits (including token and model quotas for AI workloads), policy-as-code rules on SKUs, regions and tags, approval workflows and automated actions. Maps them to SAP-C02 Task 2.6 (controls for expenditure and usage awareness) and Task 3.5 (billing alarms), the FinOps Governance, Policy & Risk capability, and AI-103's quota, rate-limit and cost-footprint objective for model and agent workloads. Azure and AWS tabs link the provider cost and governance pages. Afterwards the reader can design layered cost guardrails for a landing zone and for an AI workload.

articles.title: Cost-Aware Architecture: Designing for Cost as a Quality Attribute
articles.scope: Treats cost as a first-class quality attribute and catalogues design-to-cost patterns: rightsizing and elasticity, scale-to-zero and serverless break-even, storage tiering and lifecycle, minimising data transfer, caching, multi-tenant isolation tiers, workload placement and sustainability. Includes cost fitness functions and ADR examples. Maps the patterns to both WAF cost optimization pillars and to the FinOps Architecting & Workload Placement and Usage Optimization capabilities. Links the usage-optimization, data-transfer and sustainability articles for the operational side. Afterwards the reader can model the cost impact of an architecture choice and defend it.

articles.title: TCO, ROI and the Cloud Business Case
articles.scope: Builds a TCO model (direct, indirect and hidden costs; licensing; staff; facilities) and a business case with cash flows, ROI, NPV and payback period. The case includes CapEx-to-OpEx effects, the migration bubble of dual running, and non-financial benefits, with worked examples for a migration and for an AI solution. Compares provider outputs (Azure Migrate business case, the MAP Assess TCO model, AWS Migration Evaluator, AWS Transform assessments) with an independent model and notes their typical biases. Afterwards the reader can evaluate TCO for SAP-C02 Task 4.1, select ROI criteria and create an ROI analysis for AB-100, and present the case to finance.

articles.title: FinOps for AI and Agentic Workloads
articles.scope: Applies FinOps to AI: token-based versus provisioned-throughput pricing, GPU capacity commitments, cost drivers in RAG pipelines and agent loops, and unit economics per inference or agent task. Covers model routing (AB-100's model router), prompt caching and batching, quotas, rate limits and budgets (AI-103), and operational efficiency for generative AI applications (AIP-C01). Also covers the AI technology category in the FinOps Framework. Links ai/platforms for Microsoft Foundry, Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing, and ai/evaluation-ops for cost telemetry. Afterwards the reader can estimate and govern the cost of an agentic application.

articles.title: Running a FinOps Practice: Teams, Governance, Maturity and Executive Alignment
articles.scope: Covers the Manage the FinOps Practice domain: practice operations; Governance, Policy & Risk; FinOps assessment and maturity; education and enablement; automation, tools and services; invoicing and chargeback; and onboarding workloads, a 2025 capability whose place in the 2026 Framework must be confirmed. Also covers intersecting disciplines (ITAM, ITFM/TBM, ITSM, security, sustainability) and the new Executive Strategy Alignment capability. Shows how a central FinOps team works with platform teams, finance, procurement and leadership, and how policies become cost guardrails. Afterwards the reader can design a FinOps operating model and a maturity roadmap.

articles.title: Enterprise Architecture Fundamentals and EA Frameworks Compared
articles.scope: Defines the enterprise and enterprise architecture, its purpose and benefits, the business, data, application and technology domains, and how EA relates to solution and software architecture. Explains the practitioner's context: how EA works with business and strategic planning, portfolio and project management, operations and service management (ITSM/ITIL), solution development and enterprise risk management. Compares TOGAF, Zachman, FEAF, DoDAF, NAF and pragmatic approaches. Links security architecture frameworks such as SABSA and the TOGAF security guidance to security/grc. Positions iSAQB as a software-architecture curriculum rather than an EA framework. Afterwards the reader can explain what EA is for and choose a framework that fits an organisation.

articles.title: The TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition: Structure, Core Concepts and the Open Group Library
articles.scope: Explains TOGAF 10's modular structure (Fundamental Content and Series Guides) and how to navigate The Open Group Library to find the document that answers a question. Covers the core concepts with key definitions: EA capability, the ADM, deliverables, artifacts and building blocks, the Enterprise Continuum, the Architecture Repository, architecture principles and architecture governance. Contrasts TOGAF 10 with 9.2 and explains how to adapt the standard. Afterwards the reader can explain TOGAF's core concepts accurately and find the relevant Fundamental Content or Series Guide for a practical question.

articles.title: The TOGAF ADM: Phases, Objectives, Outputs, Iteration and Levels
articles.scope: Walks through the ADM cycle and the central Requirements Management process, giving each phase's objectives, key inputs, steps and outputs. The phases are Preliminary; A Architecture Vision; B Business; C Information Systems (Data and Application); D Technology; E Opportunities and Solutions; F Migration Planning; G Implementation Governance; and H Architecture Change Management. Explains iteration cycles, scoping, partitioning, the Strategic, Segment and Capability levels used to organise the Architecture Landscape, and how to adapt the ADM; agile adaptations are covered in ea-for-agile-and-digital-enterprises. Afterwards the reader can state the purpose and outputs of every phase and explain how the ADM is applied iteratively.

articles.title: The ADM in Practice I: Preliminary, Architecture Vision and Phases B–D
articles.scope: A scenario-driven guide to establishing the EA capability and principles, responding to a Request for Architecture Work, applying the stakeholder management technique, assessing business transformation readiness, and creating the Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work. Continues with baseline and target Business, Data, Application and Technology Architectures, choosing between alternatives, the Architecture Definition Document and Architecture Requirements Specification, gap analysis and candidate roadmap components. Afterwards the reader can plan and run Phases A–D for a given transformation.

articles.title: The ADM in Practice II: Phases E–H and Requirements Management
articles.scope: Covers consolidating gaps into work packages and Transition Architectures, migration planning and the Implementation and Migration Plan, and implementation governance with the Implementation Governance Model, Architecture Contracts, compliance reviews and dispensations. Also covers Phase H change requests and their classification (simplification, incremental, re-architecting), and requirements management across the cycle with Requirements Impact Assessments. Connects these phases to cloud migration waves and Well-Architected reviews. Afterwards the reader can plan transitions, govern implementation and manage architecture change in a realistic programme.

articles.title: TOGAF ADM Techniques Reference
articles.scope: A reference for the ADM techniques: architecture principles, stakeholder management, architecture patterns, gap analysis, migration planning, interoperability requirements, business transformation readiness assessment, risk management (initial versus residual risk), architecture alternatives and trade-offs, and capability-based planning. Also covers Series Guide techniques such as business scenarios. Gives templates and shows where each technique is used in the cycle. Links Architecture Alternatives and Trade-Offs to architecture-analysis-and-evaluation and Architecture Patterns to architecture/patterns. The chapter list must be verified against the TOGAF 10 ADM Techniques document before publication. Afterwards the reader can select and apply the right technique in each phase.

articles.title: Architecture Content, Building Blocks, the Enterprise Continuum and the Architecture Repository
articles.scope: Defines the Architecture Content Framework and content metamodel, and separates deliverables, artifacts (catalogs, matrices, diagrams) and building blocks. Contrasts Architecture Building Blocks with Solution Building Blocks. Covers the Enterprise Continuum, with the Architecture and Solutions Continua and their four levels, and the components of the Architecture Repository. Afterwards the reader can classify any architecture output correctly and organise a repository.

articles.title: Reference Architectures and Reference Models: TOGAF TRM, Industry Models and Cloud Reference Architectures
articles.scope: Separates reference models, reference architectures, patterns and Well-Architected guidance, and places them on the Enterprise Continuum levels: Foundation, Common Systems, Industry and Organization-Specific. Covers TOGAF's Technical Reference Model and III-RM, industry models such as BIAN and TM Forum's Open Digital Architecture, and cloud reference architectures from the Azure Architecture Center and AWS Architecture Center. Treats reference architectures as the technological constraints that CPSA-F LG 02-02 rates R1. Shows how to choose and tailor a reference architecture in Phase D and record the deviations. Afterwards the reader can use a reference architecture as a starting point without blindly inheriting its assumptions.

articles.title: Business Architecture: Capability Maps, Value Streams and Capability-Based Planning
articles.scope: Shows how to define business capabilities, build and heat-map a capability map, model value streams and cross-map them to capabilities, and use the result for capability-based planning and investment decisions. Contrasts capabilities with processes, functions and organisation units, and TOGAF/BIZBOK value streams with Lean value stream mapping. Afterwards the reader can produce a capability map that links strategy to applications and cloud initiatives.

articles.title: Application Portfolio Management and Rationalization
articles.scope: Teaches how to build and maintain an application inventory with business value, technical fitness, cost and risk attributes, rationalise it with TIME and lifecycle analysis, and map applications to capabilities. Contrasts ongoing APM with a one-off migration portfolio assessment, and shows how APM outputs seed migration-strategy decisions. Afterwards the reader can run a rationalization exercise that feeds both EA roadmaps and migration waves.

articles.title: Modelling the Enterprise: ArchiMate 3.2 and EA Repository Tooling
articles.scope: Introduces ArchiMate 3.2 (published October 2022; confirm it is still the current edition before publication): its layers and aspects, core and motivation elements (stakeholder, driver, assessment, goal, outcome, principle, requirement, constraint, meaning, value), relationships and viewpoints. Contrasts ArchiMate with C4, UML and BPMN. Surveys EA tooling categories (ArchiMate modellers, EA management platforms, diagrams-as-code), and shows how to keep a repository current from cloud inventories such as Azure Resource Graph and AWS Config. Afterwards the reader can model a chain from motivation and capability to technology, and choose a tool category.

articles.title: Enterprise Architecture for Agile and Digital Enterprises: Enabling Enterprise Agility, Open Agile Architecture and Architectural Runway
articles.scope: Explains how the TOGAF approach supports agile delivery and digital enterprises, as both TOGAF certifications expect. Covers architecture at different levels and speeds, iteration and partitioning matched to agile cadences, the TOGAF Series Guides on enterprise agility and the digital enterprise, and The Open Group's Open Agile Architecture standard. Contrasts EA-led governance with team-level emergent design. Connects the architectural runway, product operating models and platform teams to ADM outputs. Afterwards the reader can adapt the ADM for an organisation that delivers through agile product teams.

articles.title: Case Study: An EA-Led Multicloud Transformation from ADM to Migration Waves
articles.scope: Follows a fictional insurer from a Request for Architecture Work through capability mapping, target architectures on Azure and AWS, migration-strategy decisions and wave plans, Well-Architected reviews used as compliance checkpoints, and FinOps unit-cost targets. Shows where TOGAF, CAF, WAF and FinOps artefacts meet and where they conflict, for example Transition Architectures versus migration waves. Afterwards the reader can connect enterprise, solution and cloud architecture artefacts in one programme.

terms.definition: The fundamental structures of a software system, made up of its building blocks, their relationships and their externally visible properties, together with the principles and decisions that govern its design and evolution.

The architecture of a specific solution, often spanning several applications, services and platforms, that meets a defined business need within the principles and constraints set by enterprise architecture.
An individual, team or organisation, or a class of these, with an interest in or concerns about a system or its architecture.

An interest that one or more stakeholders hold in a system, such as cost, security, time to market or compliance. The architecture and its description must address it, although not every concern becomes a requirement.
A requirement whose satisfaction has a measurable, broad effect on the architecture, so that the architecture would probably look substantially different without it.
A requirement that states a behaviour or function the system must provide, such as an operation, calculation or data transformation, as distinct from how well it must perform.
A requirement that states how well a system must perform or which conditions it must respect, such as response time, availability or regulatory obligations, rather than which functions it provides.
A measurable or testable property of a system, such as availability, performance efficiency, security or maintainability, that shows how well it meets stakeholder needs beyond its functionality.

A non-negotiable condition that narrows the design space. It may be technical, organisational, regulatory or a convention, such as a mandated cloud provider, a budget ceiling or a data-residency rule.

A statement taken as true for design purposes without proof, such as an expected load or a partner API's stability. iSAQB requires assumptions to be made explicit and tracked, because implicit assumptions cause misunderstandings.

A structured, testable statement of a quality requirement. iSAQB uses four parts (context, stimulus, response and measurement) plus a method of analysis, while the SEI form has six (source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response and response measure).

The ISO/IEC standard that defines a product quality model. Its 2023 edition has nine characteristics (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility and safety), each refined into subcharacteristics.

The arc42 quality model, which tags quality requirements with nine top-level qualities (efficient, flexible, maintainable, operable, reliable, safe, secure, suitable and usable) used as flat, overlapping labels rather than a fixed hierarchy.

The 2023 ISO/IEC SQuaRE standard that adapts the ISO/IEC 25010 quality models to AI systems. It adds or modifies subcharacteristics such as functional adaptability, functional correctness, robustness, user controllability, transparency, intervenability, and societal and ethical risk mitigation.
aliases: SQuaRE quality model for AI systems

terms.definition: The observation that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, because people optimise the number rather than the quality it was meant to indicate.
An ATAM artefact that refines a system's overall 'utility' into quality attributes, refinements and concrete scenarios, each ranked by business importance and technical risk.
An SEI facilitated method in which stakeholders elicit, prioritise and refine quality attribute scenarios early, before a software architecture exists.

An SEI scenario-based evaluation method in which stakeholders prioritise quality attribute scenarios and evaluators analyse the architectural approaches against them, exposing risks, non-risks, sensitivity points and trade-off points.
An SEI method that extends ATAM by estimating the costs, benefits and schedule implications of architectural strategies, so that they can be ranked by return on investment.
An SEI method that combines active design reviews with ATAM-style scenarios to evaluate a partial design, such as an interface or component, while it is still being developed.
A lightweight, visual technique in which team members independently mark risks on shared architecture diagrams, then consolidate and prioritise them by impact and likelihood.

In architecture evaluation, a decision that may lead to undesirable consequences for a quality attribute. ATAM also reports non-risks (decisions judged safe) and risk themes that group systemic risks for sponsors.
A property of one or more components or design decisions that is critical for achieving a particular quality attribute response.
A design property or decision that is a sensitivity point for two or more quality attributes, so that improving one degrades another.

A short document that captures one architecturally significant decision with its context, the options considered, the decision taken and its consequences, and is kept in an append-only log alongside the system.

An open Markdown template for decision records, at version 4.0.0 since 2024-09-17, that extends the classic ADR with optional decision drivers, considered options with pros and cons, consequences and a confirmation section.
aliases: formerly: Markdown Any Decision Records (3.x naming)

terms.definition: A one-sentence decision record format: 'In the context of <situation>, facing <concern>, we decided for <option> and neglected <alternatives>, to achieve <qualities>, accepting <downsides>'.

A notation- and tool-independent way of diagramming software architecture at four levels of zoom (system context, container, component and code), supplemented by system landscape, dynamic and deployment diagrams.

In the C4 model, a separately runnable or deployable unit that executes code or stores data, such as a web application, API, serverless function, database or blob store, whether or not it is packaged as an OCI/Docker container.
In the C4 model, a grouping of related functionality behind a well-defined interface that runs inside a container and is not separately deployable.

The Object Management Group's general-purpose modelling language, currently version 2.5.1. It defines structure diagrams, such as class, package, component and deployment diagrams, and behaviour diagrams, such as sequence, activity and state machine diagrams.
The OMG standard notation (BPMN 2.0, also ISO/IEC 19510) for modelling business processes as flows of activities, events and gateways across participants.

An open-source template that organises software architecture documentation into twelve sections: introduction and goals, constraints, context and scope, solution strategy, building block view, runtime view, deployment view, crosscutting concepts, architecture decisions, quality requirements, risks and technical debt, and glossary.

In ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, a work product that expresses the architecture of an entity of interest for its stakeholders. It is organised into views that are governed by viewpoints and that address identified concerns.
A representation of a whole system from the perspective of a related set of stakeholder concerns, built according to the conventions of a viewpoint.
A specification of the conventions for building and interpreting one kind of architecture view: the concerns it addresses, its model kinds, notations and analysis techniques.

In Rozanski and Woods' approach, a collection of activities, tactics and guidelines for achieving a quality property, such as security or performance, that must be applied across several architectural views.
Philippe Kruchten's 1995 model that describes a software architecture through logical, process, development and physical views, unified and validated by a fifth set of scenarios.
Designing an architecture by developing several complementary views in parallel and keeping them consistent, for example context, building block, runtime and deployment views or Kruchten's 4+1 views.
An architectural view that shows the system as a black box together with its users, neighbouring systems and external interfaces; arc42 separates it into business context and technical context.
An architectural view that shows the static decomposition of a system into building blocks and their dependencies, refined hierarchically from black-box to white-box levels.
An architectural view that shows how building blocks interact at run time to fulfil important scenarios, using sequence or activity diagrams, numbered step lists or state machines.
An architectural view that maps building blocks or other software artefacts onto technical infrastructure, such as nodes, containers, networks and cloud services, across environments.

Two complementary descriptions of a building block: the black box gives its responsibility, interfaces and quality characteristics without internals, and the white box shows its internal building blocks and their relationships.

A short summary of the fundamental decisions that shape a system's architecture, such as technology choices, top-level decomposition and the approaches for achieving the main quality goals, recorded in arc42 section 4.

In iSAQB and arc42 usage, any structural element of a software system, such as a module, component, package or subsystem, that has defined responsibilities and interfaces and is described in black-box and white-box form.
Writing and maintaining documentation with the same tools and workflows as code (plain-text formats, version control, review and CI publishing), so that it evolves with the system.
Defining diagrams in a text-based language, such as Structurizr DSL, PlantUML or Mermaid, so that they can be versioned, reviewed, generated and kept in step with the code.
Melvin Conway's 1968 observation that organisations design systems whose structures mirror their own communication structures.
Deliberately shaping team boundaries and communication paths to match the architecture you want, so that Conway's law works in favour of the target design.

Skelton and Pais's model that organises software teams into four types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem) interacting through three modes (collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating) to limit cognitive load and speed up flow.
The total mental effort a team must spend to own its software, made up of intrinsic, extraneous and germane load. Team Topologies treats it as a limit that should shape team and system boundaries.
The lean principle of deferring an irreversible decision until failing to decide would remove an important option, so that it is taken with the most information.
A classification of decisions into one-way doors, which are costly or impossible to reverse and deserve careful analysis, and two-way doors, which are cheap to reverse and should be taken quickly.
In the Scaled Agile Framework, the existing code, components and technical infrastructure needed to implement near-term features without excessive redesign, extended through enabler work.
An iterative SEI design method that selects architectural drivers, chooses design concepts such as patterns and tactics to satisfy them, instantiates elements and records the design decisions.
An approach in which most of a system's design is completed and approved before implementation starts.
An approach in which the design evolves incrementally from working code through refactoring and feedback, with only minimal design decided up front.
An objective, ideally automated test or measurement of how closely an architecture exhibits a desired characteristic, run continuously to protect that characteristic as the system evolves.
An approach to architecture that supports guided, incremental change across several dimensions, using fitness functions and deliberately managed coupling to keep important characteristics intact.
The implied future cost of rework (the interest) that results from choosing an expedient design or implementation now instead of a better approach that would take longer.
Martin Fowler's classification of technical debt along two axes, deliberate versus inadvertent and reckless versus prudent, which separates strategic shortcuts from carelessness.
A maintained list of known technical debt items, each with its location, cause, estimated principal and interest, risk and remediation plan, used to prioritise repayment.

The gradual divergence of an implemented system from its intended architecture as successive changes break its structural rules and decisions, degrading the qualities the architecture was meant to deliver.
Thomas McCabe's source-code metric that counts the linearly independent paths through a piece of code, used as an indicator of testing effort and maintainability risk.
Dependency metrics for a building block: afferent coupling (Ca) counts incoming dependencies, efferent coupling (Ce) counts outgoing ones, and instability is Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce).
The degree to which an implemented system follows its intended architecture and architectural decisions, assessed through code and architecture reviews or tool-supported dependency analysis.
A standing group of senior architects and stakeholders that reviews significant designs and decisions, before or during delivery, for alignment with principles, standards and strategy.

A decentralised decision practice in which anyone may take an architectural decision, provided they first seek advice from those meaningfully affected and from people with relevant expertise, usually recording the outcome as an ADR.

A preventive or detective boundary, such as a policy-as-code rule, a paved-road template or a fitness function, that keeps teams within acceptable architectural choices without a manual approval gate.
A general, enduring rule that guides architecture decisions. It is documented with a name, statement, rationale and implications so that it can be applied consistently and traded off explicitly.
A mandatory, specific rule for how something must be done or which technology must be used, such as an approved database engine or API style, that implements one or more architecture principles.
Recommended but non-mandatory guidance on applying a principle or standard, from which teams may depart with justification.
A decision tool that scores options against weighted criteria and sums the weighted scores, making the basis for a selection explicit and comparable.

A periodically published visual assessment, popularised by Thoughtworks, that places technologies, tools, platforms and techniques in rings such as adopt, trial, assess and hold to steer technology choices.

Gregor Hohpe's metaphor for an architect who moves between the 'penthouse' of business strategy and the 'engine room' of technical implementation, translating decisions and their consequences in both directions.
A measurable value, tracked against a target, that shows how effectively an organisation, practice or system is achieving a key objective, such as cost per transaction or commitment coverage.

A vendor's codified architectural best practice for designing and reviewing individual workloads, organised into quality pillars with design principles, review questions or checklists and recommendations.

Microsoft's workload design framework, built on five pillars (Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence and Performance Efficiency). Each pillar provides design principles, checklists, key design strategies, tradeoffs, mapped design patterns and a five-level maturity model. The framework is extended by workload guidance, service guides, design guides and the Azure Well-Architected Review.

AWS's best practices and review questions, organised into six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability), extended by lenses and applied through Well-Architected Framework Reviews in the AWS Well-Architected Tool.

Microsoft's Well-Architected guidance for Power Platform workloads, organised into five pillars (Reliability, Security, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency and Experience Optimization) with no Cost Optimization pillar. It provides design principles, checklists, recommendations, tradeoffs and an assessment tool.
One of the top-level quality dimensions of a Well-Architected framework, such as reliability or cost optimization, each with its own design principles, practices and review questions.

The Azure Well-Architected Framework's phased adoption model. It defines five levels per pillar (establish a solid foundation on Azure, build workload assets, be production-ready, learn from production, future-proof with agility) and has its own assessment.
terms.equivalent: aws: none; AWS tracks progress through Well-Architected Tool milestones and risk counts (none)

terms.definition: The sixth AWS Well-Architected pillar, added in 2021, which aims to minimise the environmental impact of workloads by reducing energy consumption and the total resources provisioned.
terms.equivalent: azure: sustainability workload guidance in the Azure Well-Architected Framework, not a pillar (partial)

terms.definition: An extension to the AWS Well-Architected Framework that adds questions and best practices for a specific technology, industry or workload type, such as Serverless Applications, SaaS, Generative AI or Financial Services Industry, and is applied to workloads in the AWS Well-Architected Tool.
terms.equivalent: azure: Azure Well-Architected workload guidance and service guides (partial)

terms.definition: A lens authored by a customer in the AWS Well-Architected Tool, defined in a JSON lens format with its own pillars, questions, best practices, risk rules and improvement guidance, and published and shared to review workloads against internal standards.
terms.equivalent: azure: no documented equivalent; the Azure Well-Architected Review has no user-authored question sets (none)

terms.definition: AWS's structured review of a workload against the Well-Architected Framework, run in three stages: prepare (workload and scope, people and culture, documentation and infrastructure), run the review, and improve (identify risks, determine prescriptive solutions, prioritise, implement and track).

Microsoft's no-charge assessment: a set of questionnaires tied to the Azure Well-Architected Framework pillar checklists that scores a workload's design choices and produces recommendations, which can be tracked across repeated runs.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Well-Architected Tool and Well-Architected Framework Review (partial)

terms.definition: The prioritised list of remediation actions produced by a Well-Architected review. It links each high- or medium-risk issue to the recommended best practices and is tracked through milestones until resolved.
In an AWS Well-Architected review, a gap against best practice that could significantly harm the business; it is listed in the improvement plan for priority remediation.
terms.equivalent: azure: high-priority recommendations in the Azure Well-Architected Review (partial)

terms.definition: In an AWS Well-Architected review, a gap against best practice that could harm the business but is less severe than a high-risk issue.
terms.equivalent: azure: medium-priority recommendations in the Azure Well-Architected Review (partial)

terms.definition: A set of components (code, configuration, data and infrastructure) that together deliver a specific business capability; it is the main unit for Well-Architected reviews, migration waves and cost allocation.

The Green Software Foundation specification, standardised as ISO/IEC 21031:2024, that expresses a software system's emissions as a rate per functional unit, SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R. E is the energy used, I is the grid's carbon intensity and M is embodied emissions.

The Greenhouse Gas Protocol's classification of emissions into Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased energy) and Scope 3 (other value-chain emissions). A customer's cloud usage normally falls within its Scope 3.
Shifting when or where flexible workloads run, guided by grid carbon-intensity data, so that they use electricity with lower carbon intensity.

A provider's organisation-level guidance for planning and carrying out cloud adoption across strategy, people, governance, platform, security and operations, as distinct from workload-level Well-Architected guidance.

terms.term: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure
terms.definition: Microsoft's guidance for Azure adoption, organised into seven phases (Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure and Manage) and extended by scenarios such as AI adoption, AI agents, data platform, sovereignty and Azure VMware Solution.

AWS guidance that groups foundational capabilities into six perspectives (Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations). It drives transformation through the Envision, Align, Launch and Scale phases across the technology, process, organization and product domains.

terms.term: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for AI
terms.definition: An AWS whitepaper that extends the AWS CAF's perspectives and foundational capabilities with AI-, ML- and generative-AI-specific capabilities and a transformation journey for organisations adopting AI.
aliases: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Generative AI
terms.equivalent: azure: CAF AI adoption and AI agents scenarios (partial)

terms.definition: How an organisation divides cloud responsibilities (governance, security, platform and workload operations) between central and workload teams, commonly as a centralized, shared-management or decentralized model.

A cross-functional team of cloud experts that drives adoption by defining standards, reusable patterns, platform services and enablement for workload teams, and that often evolves into a platform team.

A cross-functional team that sets AI strategy, governance, responsible-AI standards, platform choices and reusable assets, and enables business units to adopt AI consistently, as Microsoft's CAF AI adoption guidance and AB-100 describe.
In Microsoft's CAF, the business, IT, finance and security leaders who set the cloud adoption motivations, objectives and priorities and remain accountable for executing the strategy.

An operating model that funds and organises long-lived, cross-functional teams around products or value streams with continuous ownership of outcomes, instead of temporary project teams that hand over to operations.
A team that builds and runs internal platforms, such as landing zones, shared services and paved roads, as products that workload teams consume through self-service.
The team accountable for designing, building and operating a specific workload end to end, within the guardrails and shared services that central or platform teams provide.

The treatment chosen for an individual workload when moving to the cloud (retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase or replace, refactor, rearchitect or rebuild), based on its business driver, risk and value.

A migration strategy that moves a workload like-for-like without changing its code or architecture, typically servers to IaaS virtual machines. In Microsoft's CAF it also covers IaaS-to-IaaS and PaaS-to-PaaS moves, such as AWS Elastic Beanstalk to Azure App Service.

An AWS 7 Rs strategy that moves servers or resources to a cloud-hosted version of the same platform, such as VMware Cloud Foundation on Amazon Elastic VMware Service, or between VPCs, Regions or accounts, without buying hardware, rewriting applications or changing operations.
terms.equivalent: azure: no CAF strategy of that name; like-for-like VMware moves follow the Azure VMware Solution scenario (partial)

terms.definition: A migration strategy that moves a workload with targeted optimisations, such as adopting a managed database, PaaS hosting or containers, while keeping its core architecture and most of its code.

A migration strategy whose meaning depends on the framework. AWS's 'refactor or re-architect' redesigns a workload around cloud-native features, while Microsoft's CAF uses refactor for code changes that reduce technical debt or optimise for the cloud without changing the architecture.

A migration strategy, listed separately in Microsoft's CAF, that redesigns a workload's architecture, for example by splitting a monolith into services, to gain cloud-native capabilities such as independent scaling.
A CAF migration strategy that redevelops a workload from scratch as a cloud-native solution instead of carrying its legacy code forward.
A migration strategy that replaces an application with a different product, typically a SaaS offering, instead of moving the existing software.
A migration strategy that decommissions or archives a workload that no longer delivers enough business value to justify migrating it.

A migration strategy that deliberately keeps a workload where it is for now, because of compliance, dependencies, recent investment or low return, and schedules it for later review; CAF suggests managing such workloads with hybrid tools such as Azure Arc.

A structured analysis of an organisation's applications and infrastructure (inventory, dependencies, utilisation, business value, technical fit and cost) used to choose migration strategies, priorities and waves.
An AWS CAF-based assessment, run in the MAP Assess phase, that scores an organisation's readiness to migrate across the CAF perspectives and produces a gap list and action plan.
terms.equivalent: azure: CAF 'assess migration readiness and skills' step and Azure Migrate business case (partial)

terms.definition: Discovering network and application dependencies between servers and services with agent-based or agentless collection, and classifying them (CAF: direct, indirect or business), so that interdependent components migrate together.
A set of tightly interdependent servers and applications that must be migrated and cut over together; one or more move groups make up a migration wave.
A scheduled batch of workloads, made up of move groups, that is migrated and cut over together within one time-boxed iteration of a migration programme.
A scaled, repeatable migration operating model in which dedicated teams, standard runbooks, automation and metrics move workloads through intake, migration and cutover like a production line.

The planned event in which production traffic, data ownership and operations switch from the source environment to the target, governed by go/no-go criteria, a rollback plan and a following hypercare period.
A formal checkpoint before cutover at which stakeholders compare readiness evidence with agreed success criteria and decide whether to proceed, delay or roll back.
A pre-approved, tested procedure with explicit trigger criteria for returning a workload to its source or previous known-good state when a migration or deployment fails.

A time-boxed period of heightened monitoring and support immediately after cutover, during which the migration team stays engaged to stabilise the workload before it is handed to business-as-usual operations.

A migration in which the source stays in service while an initial copy is made and ongoing changes are replicated continuously, typically by change data capture, so that cutover needs only a short downtime window.
A migration in which the source is stopped or frozen while its data is copied to the target, accepting downtime for the whole transfer in exchange for simplicity and consistency.
differs_from: offline data transfer by shipped devices
