terms.definition: A database migration between different engines, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, that requires converting schemas, code objects and data types as well as moving the data.

A database migration between the same or compatible engines, for example SQL Server to Azure SQL Managed Instance or MySQL to Amazon RDS for MySQL, in which schemas move largely unchanged and native tools can be used.
The temporary rise in spend during a migration, when migration effort overlaps with running the source and target environments in parallel, before decommissioning savings arrive.

AWS's migration programme. Its Assess phase produces a CAF-based readiness assessment and a TCO model, Mobilize closes gaps and builds the operational foundation, and Migrate & Modernize executes. It combines methodology, tools, partner and AWS expertise and funding, with variants for Microsoft, VMware, SAP and mainframe workloads.

Microsoft's migration and AI-innovation programme for Azure. It combines free Microsoft expert help through the Cloud Accelerate Factory, specialized-partner funding, Azure credits, pricing offers and skilling in a plan-then-execute approach (assessment, business case or proof of value; then landing zone and migrate or build), with add-ons such as Frontier Accelerate for Databases.
aliases: formerly: Azure Migrate and Modernize offer

terms.definition: A documented, tested plan for moving workloads and data off a cloud provider or service, to another provider or back on premises. It covers triggers, target options, data export, contract terms, timelines and costs.
Dependence on a provider's proprietary services, data formats, APIs, contracts or skills that makes switching costly or slow, measured by the effort and cost of exit.

In ISO/IEC 17788 and CCSP usage, the ability of a cloud customer to retrieve its data and application artefacts, and to have the provider delete the customer's data within an agreed period, so that it can leave a service without loss.
Moving workloads or data from public cloud back to on-premises or private infrastructure, typically for reasons of cost, performance, sovereignty or control.

An operational framework and cultural practice that maximises the business value of cloud and technology, enables timely data-driven decisions, and creates financial accountability through collaboration between engineering, finance and business teams.

The FinOps Framework's six principles: teams need to collaborate; business value drives technology decisions; everyone takes ownership of their technology usage; FinOps data should be accessible, timely and accurate; FinOps should be enabled centrally; and take advantage of the variable cost model of the cloud.

The roles the FinOps Framework expects to work together. The core personas are FinOps practitioner, engineering, finance, product, procurement and leadership; allied personas include ITAM, ITFM/TBM, ITSM, sustainability and security teams.

The three iterative phases FinOps teams cycle through: Inform (visibility, allocation, benchmarking, budgeting and forecasting), Optimize (rate and usage efficiency) and Operate (KPIs, governance and continuous improvement).
The FinOps Framework's Crawl, Walk, Run scale for judging how mature a practice is, applied capability by capability rather than as one rating for the whole organisation.

One of the four top-level areas of the FinOps Framework (Understand Usage & Cost, Quantify Business Value, Optimize Usage & Cost, and Manage the FinOps Practice), each grouping related capabilities around an outcome.
A functional area of FinOps activity within a domain, such as Allocation, Forecasting or Rate Optimization, described by its purpose, personas, maturity characteristics and KPIs.

A defined segment of technology spend, aligned to business constructs and drawing on technology categories such as public cloud, SaaS, data center, licensing or AI, to which FinOps capabilities, personas and KPIs are applied.
differs_from: Azure scope (management group, subscription or resource group)

terms.definition: Assigning technology costs to the teams, products, cost centres or customers responsible for them, using account or subscription hierarchies, tags or labels, and rules for splitting shared costs.
Splitting costs that serve several consumers, such as shared platforms, support charges or untaggable spend, by an even split, a proportional usage-weighted split or fixed agreed percentages.
Reporting allocated costs to the teams that incur them, to build awareness and accountability, without moving money between their budgets.
Billing allocated costs to the consuming teams' budgets through internal accounting entries, so that each business unit's financial results carry the cost of its technology usage.

A governed scheme of required tag or label keys, allowed values, ownership and enforcement that attributes resources to owners, cost centres, environments and applications for allocation, automation and governance.
Measuring technology cost against a business-relevant unit of value, such as cost per customer, transaction, tenant or AI inference, to judge efficiency and margin as volume changes.
A reduction in future spend that would otherwise have occurred, such as rightsizing before a planned scale-out, reported separately from cost savings because it does not lower the current baseline.
Lowering the price paid per unit of usage, without changing how much is consumed, through commitment discounts, negotiated agreements, licensing choices and the choice of pricing model.
Reducing the quantity of resources consumed, by rightsizing, scheduling, scaling, removing idle resources and choosing efficient architectures, so that usage matches business demand.
Changing the size, type or tier of a resource to match its observed utilisation and performance requirements, removing over- or under-provisioning.
A lower price granted in exchange for committing to a quantity of usage or an amount of spend over a term, typically one or three years, as with reservations and savings plans.
A commitment discount tied to a quantity of a specific resource type, often also a region or instance family, over a term; Azure reservations and AWS Reserved Instances are examples.

A commitment to an hourly amount of spend that is applied to eligible usage. Its flexibility ranges from one instance family in one Region (AWS EC2 Instance Savings Plans) to many services and Regions (AWS Compute or Database Savings Plans, Azure savings plans).
A contractual commitment to spend a total amount with a provider over a multi-year term in exchange for organisation-wide discounts or credits.

A reservation that guarantees compute capacity of a given type in a specific zone or region while it is held. It is billed at on-demand rates whether used or not and gives no discount of its own, although commitment discounts can apply to it.
Spare provider capacity sold at deep discounts that the provider can reclaim at short notice, suited to fault-tolerant workloads that can be interrupted.
The percentage of a purchased commitment's capacity or spend actually consumed in a period; the unused remainder is still paid for but delivers no value.
The percentage of eligible usage or spend in a period that commitment discounts covered, rather than being billed at on-demand rates.
The percentage saved on eligible spend compared with what the same usage would have cost at on-demand rates, net of unused commitments, so that it reflects both discount depth and utilisation.
The level of utilisation, or the point in the term, at which a commitment's total cost equals the on-demand cost of the usage it covers; below that point the commitment loses money.

terms.term: FOCUS (FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification)
terms.definition: An open FinOps Foundation specification that defines a common schema, columns and terminology for billing and usage data from cloud, SaaS and other technology providers. Version 1.4 was released in June 2026.
aliases: FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification

terms.definition: In FOCUS, the cost of a charge at the provider's public list unit price multiplied by the pricing quantity, before any negotiated or commitment discounts.
In FOCUS, the cost of a charge at the contracted unit price: it includes negotiated discounts but excludes commitment discounts.
A cost view that spreads upfront and recurring commitment purchases across the usage they cover during the term, so that each period and resource shows its effective consumption cost.
The amount actually charged on an invoice for a period. It records commitment purchases when they are billed rather than spreading them over the usage they discount.
Detecting, alerting on, investigating and resolving unexpected deviations of cost or usage from expected patterns before they add up to significant overspend.
An approved spending limit for a scope and period, tracked against actual and forecast cost with threshold alerts or automated actions.
A projection of future technology cost and usage, based on historical trends and business drivers, used to set budgets and catch variance early.

A preventive or detective control that keeps technology spend within agreed limits without manual review of every change, such as a budget alert, quota, policy-as-code rule, approval workflow or automated action.
Charges for moving data between availability zones, regions, services, on-premises networks and the internet; they vary by direction and path and are largely set by architecture choices.

Using software licences the customer already owns, such as Windows Server or SQL Server licences with Software Assurance or subscriptions, on cloud resources, so that the cloud price excludes the licence component, within each vendor's licence-mobility rules.

The practice of tracking and managing hardware, software and cloud assets through their lifecycle, including the software licences and entitlements covered by software asset management, to control cost, risk and compliance.

A discipline and standard taxonomy for IT financial management that maps costs from the general ledger to IT resources, towers, solutions and consumers, so that technology spend can be managed by business value.

The full lifetime cost of acquiring, operating and retiring a solution, including direct, indirect and often hidden costs such as staff, facilities, licences and downtime, used to compare on-premises and cloud options.
A ratio that compares an investment's net benefit with its cost, (benefits − costs) ÷ costs, used to compare options and justify business cases.
The sum of an investment's future net cash flows discounted to today at a chosen rate, minus the initial investment; a positive NPV means the investment creates value at that rate.
The time it takes for cumulative net benefits to recover an investment's initial cost; it ignores the time value of money and any benefits after that point.

The discipline of describing an enterprise's current and target business, data, application and technology structures and their relationships, and of guiding change between them in line with strategy.

One of the broad areas into which an enterprise architecture is divided for development; TOGAF uses four (business, data, application and technology), with data and application together forming the Information Systems Architectures.

A representation of holistic, multi-dimensional business views (capabilities, end-to-end value delivery, information and organisational structure), and of the relationships between these views and strategies, products, policies, initiatives and stakeholders.
In TOGAF, a description of the structure and interaction of applications as groups of capabilities that provide key business functions and manage the data assets.
In TOGAF, a description of the structure and interaction of the technology services and technology components, such as platforms, networks and hosting, that support the applications.

The Open Group's open enterprise architecture standard, now in its 10th Edition, made up of the TOGAF Fundamental Content and the TOGAF Series Guides and centred on the Architecture Development Method.

Supplementary documents of the TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition, published in The Open Group Library, that explain how to apply the Fundamental Content to specific topics such as business capabilities, value streams, business scenarios, the digital enterprise and agility.

An organisation's ability to undertake enterprise architecture effectively, made up of its EA organisation, roles, skills, processes, governance, repository and tools; it is established in the Preliminary phase.
TOGAF's iterative method for developing and managing an enterprise architecture, made up of the Preliminary phase and Phases A to H arranged around a central Requirements Management process.

The groupings of ADM phases that TOGAF suggests iterating together: architecture context (Preliminary and A), architecture definition (B to D), transition planning (E and F) and architecture governance (G and H).

Dividing the enterprise architecture into separately managed parts by subject matter, time, maturity or volatility, level of detail or viewpoint, so that teams can work in parallel and conflicts between architectures can be managed.

A short, high-level description of the Target Architecture, its business value and the changes it will bring, produced in ADM Phase A to win stakeholder buy-in and bound the detailed architecture work.

The TOGAF deliverable, produced in Phase A, that defines the scope, approach, plan, roles and acceptance criteria of an architecture project; once signed, it is the agreement between the architecture team and its sponsors.
The document a sponsoring organisation sends to the architecture function to start an ADM cycle, describing the business drivers, scope, constraints and resources for the requested work.

A TOGAF technique, typically applied in Phase A, that evaluates and quantifies an organisation's readiness for change using factors such as vision, sponsorship, need, funding, governance and skills, and feeds the results into risk management and migration planning.

A TOGAF technique, published as a Series Guide, that describes a business problem, its environment, the actors involved and the desired outcomes, so that business requirements and SMART objectives can be derived for the architecture.
The description of an existing architecture that serves as the starting point for change, usually documented only as deeply as gap analysis needs.
The description of a desired future state of an architecture, developed to meet business goals and used to derive the gaps and the migration path from the baseline.
A formally defined intermediate state between the Baseline and Target Architectures: a stable state of the enterprise that delivers measurable business value at a point in time.
A TOGAF technique that compares Baseline and Target Architectures, typically in a gap matrix, to find which elements are kept, removed or new; the resulting gaps feed roadmaps and work packages.
A TOGAF ADM technique for identifying alternative candidate architectures, comparing them against stakeholder concerns and criteria, and recording the trade-offs that justify the option selected.

The TOGAF deliverable that holds the core architectural artifacts for a project across the business, data, application and technology domains and the relevant baseline, transition and target states. It is the qualitative view; the Architecture Requirements Specification complements it.

The TOGAF deliverable that gives quantitative, testable statements of what an implementation project must do to comply with the architecture, such as success measures, conformance requirements, constraints and service levels.
A TOGAF deliverable that places on a timeline the work packages needed to realise the Target Architecture, showing the progression through any Transition Architectures.
A set of actions identified to achieve one or more business objectives, which can be part of a project, a complete project or a programme, and is sequenced in the Architecture Roadmap.

The TOGAF deliverable, started in Phase E and completed in Phase F, that schedules the projects and work packages needed to realise the Target Architecture through any Transition Architectures, with their costs, benefits and dependencies.
A Phase F output that defines how architecture governance will oversee implementation projects, including the roles, compliance checkpoints and Architecture Contracts involved.
A joint agreement between development partners and sponsors on the deliverables, quality and fitness for purpose of an architecture, used in Implementation Governance to make sure solutions conform.

A TOGAF governance activity that examines a project's design and implementation against the architecture and rates its conformance as irrelevant, consistent, compliant, conformant, fully conformant or non-conformant.

In TOGAF, the practice and orientation by which enterprise architectures and other architectures are managed and controlled at enterprise level, through controls, compliance, accountability and an Architecture Board.
In TOGAF, the executive-backed, cross-organisational body responsible for architecture governance. It ensures consistency, enforces compliance, grants dispensations and resolves escalations.
A time-limited exception, granted by the Architecture Board, that allows a project or solution to depart from the architecture or its standards, normally with conditions and a review date.

A formal request, often raised during implementation governance, to change the architecture or a solution; Phase H assesses it and classifies it as a simplification, an incremental change or a re-architecting change.
A TOGAF Requirements Management output that assesses what a new or changed requirement means for the current architecture and states which ADM phases must be revisited.

In TOGAF's risk management technique, the classification of a risk's effect and frequency before mitigation (initial level of risk) and after mitigating actions have been applied (residual level of risk).
TOGAF's structured model for architecture outputs, which classifies work products as deliverables, artifacts and building blocks and organises them according to the content metamodel.

The TOGAF model that defines the entities of architecture content, such as actors, business services, data entities, application components and technology components, together with their attributes and relationships, so that artifacts stay consistent and traceable.
An architectural work product that is specified contractually and formally reviewed, agreed and signed off by stakeholders, such as the Architecture Definition Document.

An architectural work product that describes one aspect of the architecture and is classified as a catalog (a list of things), a matrix (relationships between things) or a diagram (a picture of things).
In TOGAF, a potentially reusable component of enterprise capability, with defined boundaries and interfaces, that can be combined with other building blocks to deliver architectures and solutions.

A TOGAF building block that captures architecture requirements and describes a required capability in product- and vendor-neutral terms, guiding the selection or development of Solution Building Blocks.
A TOGAF building block that is a candidate implementation of an Architecture Building Block: a specific product, service or configuration that can be bought or built.

TOGAF's mechanism for classifying architecture and solution assets, and a view of the Architecture Repository. It arranges assets from generic to Organization-Specific across the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum.
The part of the Enterprise Continuum that classifies architecture assets from generic to specific: Foundation, Common Systems, Industry and Organization-Specific Architectures.

The part of the Enterprise Continuum that classifies solution assets (products, services and implementations) realising the corresponding levels of the Architecture Continuum, from Foundation Solutions to Organization-Specific Solutions.

The most generic level of the Architecture Continuum: generic building blocks, their relationships, principles and guidelines that provide a base for more specific architectures; TOGAF's Technical Reference Model is an example.

The Architecture Continuum level that combines Foundation Architecture services into reusable architectures for common cross-industry problem domains, such as security, management or networking; TOGAF's III-RM is an example.

The Architecture Continuum level that combines common systems components with industry-specific ones for a particular vertical, such as BIAN for banking or TM Forum's Open Digital Architecture for telecommunications.
The most specific level of the Architecture Continuum, which describes and guides the deployment of solution components for a particular enterprise or extended enterprise.

TOGAF's structured store of architecture outputs at different levels of abstraction. Its components include the architecture metamodel, architecture capability, architecture landscape, standards, reference library, governance log, architecture requirements and solutions landscape.
The architectural representation of the building blocks in use or planned across the enterprise at a point in time, divided into Strategic, Segment and Capability levels of detail.

A generalised, reusable architecture for a class of problem or domain, such as a cloud landing zone or an e-commerce platform, that captures proven structures, patterns and decisions to be tailored for specific solutions.

An abstract framework of concepts, terms and relationships for a domain, such as TOGAF's TRM or the FEAF reference models, that is independent of specific architectures and used to classify and compare them.
TOGAF's Foundation Architecture reference model: a taxonomy and diagram of the generic application-platform services and interfaces on which more specific architectures can build.
TOGAF's Common Systems reference model, focused on the application software that delivers boundaryless information flow across an enterprise.
A particular ability that a business may possess or exchange to achieve a specific purpose, describing what the business does independently of how, where or by whom it is done.

A hierarchical model of an enterprise's business capabilities, usually drawn as nested boxes and often heat-mapped by maturity, investment or risk, used to align strategy, applications and investment.

In TOGAF and BIZBOK usage, an end-to-end collection of value-adding stages that creates an overall result for a customer, stakeholder or end user; it is used with business capabilities to plan change.
A TOGAF technique that focuses planning, engineering and delivery on strategic business capabilities, coordinating projects across architecture domains to deliver capability increments.
A TOGAF artifact that lists stakeholders, their concerns, their influence and the views they need, often using a power–interest grid to decide how to engage each group.
The Business Architecture Guild's body of knowledge, which defines business architecture concepts such as capability mapping, value stream mapping, information mapping and organisation mapping.
aliases: A Guide to the Business Architecture Body of Knowledge

terms.definition: The Open Group's open modelling language for enterprise architecture (ArchiMate 3.2, published October 2022), with a common set of elements and relationships across the strategy, business, application, technology, physical and implementation-and-migration layers, plus motivation elements such as stakeholders, drivers, goals, principles and requirements.
The Open Group's standard for architecting agile, digital enterprises, which combines agile and lean practices with architecture across strategy, organisation, product, operations and technology.

John Zachman's two-dimensional ontology that classifies descriptions of an enterprise by six interrogatives (what, how, where, who, when, why) against six stakeholder perspectives, without prescribing a method.

The US federal government's EA framework (version 2), whose consolidated reference model has six sub-models (performance, business, data, application, infrastructure and security) for aligning agency architectures.

The US Department of Defense architecture framework (version 2.02), which organises architecture descriptions into viewpoints such as capability, operational, services, systems, data and information, standards and project, on the DoDAF Meta Model (DM2).

NATO's architecture framework (version 4), which arranges viewpoints in a grid of subjects of concern against aspects and is designed to be expressed in ArchiMate or the Unified Architecture Framework.

The ongoing practice of keeping an inventory of an organisation's applications and assessing each one's business value, technical fitness, cost and risk to decide whether to invest in it, tolerate it, migrate it or eliminate it.
A Gartner application-rationalisation model that places each application in the Tolerate, Invest, Migrate or Eliminate quadrant according to its business value and technical quality.

pairs.difference: A viewpoint is the reusable specification of concerns, model kinds and notations. A view is the concrete representation of one particular system produced by applying a viewpoint.
A view describes one aspect of the system's structure or behaviour. A perspective is a quality-focused set of tactics and checks, such as security, applied across many views rather than drawn as one.
A functional requirement says what the system must do; a non-functional requirement says how well it must do it, or which conditions it must respect.

A quality attribute is a property of the system, such as availability. An NFR is a stated requirement on such a property (for example 99.95% monthly availability) or another non-behavioural condition such as GDPR compliance.
A constraint is an imposed fact the design must obey. An assumption is something believed true but unproven, which must be made explicit and validated because the design may fail if it is wrong.

ISO/IEC 25010 is a formal hierarchy of nine characteristics and their subcharacteristics. Q42 uses nine adjectives as flat tags, so one requirement can carry several, and it covers developer-facing qualities that ISO leaves out.

ISO/IEC 25010 is the general product quality model. ISO/IEC 25059 adapts it for AI systems, adding or modifying qualities such as robustness, transparency, functional adaptability and intervenability.

A Quality Attribute Workshop elicits scenarios from stakeholders before an architecture exists. A utility tree organises and ranks scenarios, by business importance and technical risk, as input to an ATAM evaluation.
A sensitivity point is critical to one quality attribute's response. A trade-off point is a sensitivity point for two or more attributes, so tuning it helps one attribute and hurts another.

ATAM is a multi-day facilitated evaluation against prioritised scenarios that produces documented risks and trade-offs. Risk storming is a short collaborative exercise of marking risks on diagrams, cheap enough to repeat every iteration.
ATAM finds the risks and trade-offs of the architectural approaches. CBAM adds costs, benefits and schedule to rank the candidate strategies by return on investment.
ARID reviews an intermediate, partial design, such as an interface, by having reviewers actively use it. ATAM evaluates a whole architecture against stakeholder-prioritised scenarios.

ATAM evaluates one architecture against quality scenarios prioritised for that system, to expose trade-offs. A Well-Architected review checks a workload against a provider's generic best-practice questions to find gaps and risks.

An ADR (Nygard or MADR) is a short document with context, options and consequences. A Y-statement compresses the same decision into one structured sentence, often used as an ADR's summary or in a decision log.

C4 is a lightweight set of zoom levels and abstractions with no prescribed notation. UML is a formal, standardised notation with many diagram types, and C4 diagrams can be drawn with UML or without it.

C4 describes the structure of one software system for developers and architects. ArchiMate models the whole enterprise, from motivation and strategy through business and applications to technology, with a formal metamodel.

A C4 container is any separately runnable or deployable unit that runs code or stores data, including databases, single-page apps and serverless functions. A Docker container is one packaging and runtime technology, so many C4 containers are not Docker containers, and the reverse.
A container is separately deployable and runs as its own process or service. A component is a grouping of code behind an interface inside a container and is deployed with it.

The building-block view shows the static structure: what the parts are and how they depend on each other. The runtime view shows the behaviour: how the parts collaborate over time to fulfil a scenario.

Conway's law describes what happens by default: system structure mirrors communication structure. The inverse Conway manoeuvre uses that effect deliberately, reorganising teams so that the desired architecture emerges.
BDUF settles most design before coding and risks building on wrong assumptions. Emergent design decides little in advance and risks costly rework on decisions that are hard to reverse.
Architectural runway builds just enough infrastructure for the next few increments and extends it continuously. BDUF tries to settle the whole design before implementation.

The last responsible moment is about when to decide: delay until waiting would close options. One-way and two-way doors are about how carefully to decide: slowly for irreversible choices, quickly for reversible ones.

Technical debt is a shortcut, often deliberate, whose future cost can be tracked and repaid. Erosion is unplanned divergence of the code from the intended architecture through accumulated rule violations, usually caught only by conformance checks.

Cyclomatic complexity measures the internal branching of a unit of code. Afferent and efferent coupling measure how a building block depends on, and is depended on by, other blocks, which is the architecture-level concern.

Conformance (iSAQB) asks whether the code follows the system's own architectural decisions and is often checked by tools. A TOGAF compliance review asks whether a project conforms to the enterprise architecture and grades it on a six-level scale.

A principle is a general, enduring rule with a rationale, such as 'prefer managed services'. A standard is a specific, mandatory choice that implements it, such as 'use Azure SQL Database or Amazon Aurora for relational data'.

An ARB centralises approval authority in a review body. The advice process leaves the decision with the people doing the work, who must only seek and record advice, trading central control for speed and ownership.

The TOGAF Architecture Board is an executive-backed governance body with formal powers over compliance, dispensations and escalations. A generic ARB is often a technical design-review forum without that enterprise mandate.

Architecture guardrails constrain design and deployment choices through policy-as-code, templates and fitness functions. AI guardrails filter model prompts and responses at runtime for safety and policy, so the same word applies at a different layer.

A solution strategy (arc42 section 4) summarises the fundamental technical decisions of one system. A TOGAF Architecture Vision is an aspirational, stakeholder-facing outline of the target enterprise architecture and its business value, produced before detailed design.

In iSAQB and arc42, a building block is any structural element of the software (module, component, subsystem). In TOGAF, a building block is a reusable package of enterprise capability, specified as an ABB and realised by SBBs, and usually much coarser-grained.
An ABB states the required capability in product-neutral terms; an SBB is the specific product, service or configuration chosen to realise it.

A deliverable is a contractually specified work product that stakeholders formally review and sign off. An artifact (catalog, matrix or diagram) describes one aspect of the architecture and is usually packaged inside deliverables.

The Architecture Definition Document describes the architecture qualitatively, through artifacts across the domains and states. The Architecture Requirements Specification states quantitatively what implementations must meet to comply.

The Architecture Roadmap lists the work packages and Transition Architectures needed to reach the target over time. The Implementation and Migration Plan turns them into scheduled, costed and resourced projects.

A change request asks for a change to the architecture or a solution and is handled in Phase H. A Requirements Impact Assessment analyses what a changed requirement means for the architecture and which phases must be revisited.

The Architecture Continuum classifies architecture specifications from generic to organisation-specific. The Solutions Continuum classifies the products, services and implementations that realise them at each matching level.

The Enterprise Continuum is a classification scheme, a way of viewing assets from generic to specific. The Architecture Repository is the actual store that holds those assets, plus the metamodel, standards, governance log and requirements.

A reference model is an abstract vocabulary and structure for a domain, such as TOGAF's TRM. A reference architecture is a reusable architecture with concrete structures and patterns that can be tailored into a solution.

A reference architecture gives a reusable design for a class of solution. A Well-Architected framework gives questions and best practices for judging any design, so a reference architecture can itself be reviewed against a WAF.

A TOGAF compliance review checks a project against the enterprise's own architecture and standards. A Well-Architected review checks a workload against a cloud provider's generic best practices, and the two can be combined at the same checkpoint.

A capability describes what the business can do, stays stable over time and is independent of organisation and technology. A process describes how work flows step by step, and it changes far more often.

Capabilities describe what the business is able to do. Value streams describe the stages through which value is delivered to a stakeholder, and they are cross-mapped to show which capabilities enable each stage.

TOGAF and BIZBOK value streams are stages of stakeholder value, cross-mapped to capabilities for strategic planning. Lean value stream mapping charts material and information flow with timings to remove waste from an operational process.

TOGAF is a comprehensive EA method built around the ADM and its governance. O-AA is The Open Group's lighter, agile-first standard for architecting digital enterprises, and it can complement TOGAF rather than replace it.
TOGAF is a method (the ADM) with content and governance guidance. Zachman is a classification schema for architecture descriptions that says nothing about how to develop them.

A Transition Architecture is a stable intermediate state of the enterprise that delivers business value. A migration wave is an execution batch of workloads, and several waves may be needed to reach one Transition Architecture.
A work package is a unit of change on the Architecture Roadmap and can be any project or programme. A migration wave is specifically a scheduled batch of workloads moved and cut over together.

TOGAF's BTRA measures organisational readiness for any business transformation using factors such as vision, sponsorship and funding. An AWS MRA measures readiness for a cloud migration specifically, across the AWS CAF perspectives.

A Well-Architected framework guides the design and review of individual workloads by quality pillar. A Cloud Adoption Framework guides the organisation's journey: strategy, operating model, landing zones, governance and migration.

Both are Microsoft frameworks with five pillars. Power Platform replaces Cost Optimization with Experience Optimization, because low-code workload costs are dominated by licensing rather than infrastructure design.

Both reward eliminating waste and improving utilisation, but they diverge on choices such as buying cheaper capacity in a carbon-intensive region or keeping idle redundancy, where the cheapest option is not the lowest-carbon one.
A high-risk issue could significantly harm the business and is remediated first. A medium-risk issue is a real gap with lower expected impact, often accepted temporarily with a documented plan.
An AWS-published lens adds AWS's own questions for a technology or industry. A custom lens is authored by the customer to encode internal standards and is shared through the WA Tool.
SCI is a rate per functional unit used to improve a software system. GHG scopes classify an organisation's total emissions inventory for reporting, so SCI drives design while scopes drive disclosure.
The strategy team is a leadership group that sets direction, objectives and priorities. The CCoE is a hands-on expert team that turns that direction into standards, platforms and enablement.
A platform team builds and runs shared foundations as products for others. A workload team owns one business workload end to end and consumes the platform.
A project model funds temporary teams to deliver scope and then hand over to operations. A product model funds long-lived teams that own outcomes, run what they build and change continuously.

A migration portfolio assessment is a time-boxed analysis to choose migration treatments, priorities and waves. Application portfolio management is a continuous EA practice that manages every application's value, fitness, cost and lifecycle.

A readiness assessment examines the organisation (skills, governance, operations, security) to see whether it can migrate. A portfolio assessment examines the workloads to decide what to migrate, how and when.
A move group is the smallest set of interdependent servers that must move together. A wave is a scheduled batch that combines several move groups for one cutover window.
Cutover is the switch itself, governed by go/no-go and rollback criteria. Hypercare is the period of intensified support that follows until the workload is stable enough for normal operations.

Rehost moves the workload as it is, for speed and low risk. Replatform makes targeted changes during the move, such as adopting a managed database, to gain cloud benefits without redesigning the architecture.
Relocate moves whole hypervisor-level estates, such as VMware, onto a cloud-hosted version of the same platform, keeping tools and operations. Rehost converts each server into a native cloud VM.

In CAF, refactor improves code internals without changing the architecture, while rearchitect changes the architecture itself, for example by splitting a monolith. AWS folds both into a single 'refactor or re-architect' strategy.
Retire removes a workload for good because it no longer earns its keep. Retain deliberately leaves it in place for now and schedules a later review.

Online (near-zero downtime) migration keeps the source live and replicates changes until a short cutover. Offline (downtime) migration stops the source for the whole copy and accepts longer downtime for simplicity. Neither is the same as offline data transfer on shipped devices.
An exit strategy is a prepared, tested plan that may never be used and may target another cloud. Repatriation is the act of actually moving workloads back to on-premises or private infrastructure.
Lock-in is the condition: the cost and effort of leaving. Reversibility is the contractual and technical capability that reduces it, through data retrieval, deletion and exit assistance.

TIME sets an application's future investment posture (tolerate, invest, migrate, eliminate) from its business value and technical quality. The 7 Rs decide how a workload is treated in a specific cloud migration, so TIME results feed 7R choices but do not replace them.
A domain is one of four outcome areas of the FinOps Framework. A capability is a specific practice within a domain, with its own maturity levels and KPIs.

Inform, Optimize and Operate are phases a team cycles through continuously. Crawl, Walk and Run describe how mature each capability is, so a team can be at Walk in one capability and Crawl in another while still cycling the lifecycle.

Showback reports allocated costs for awareness without moving money. Chargeback debits the consuming teams' budgets, which requires more accurate allocation, agreed rules for shared costs and a dispute process.

Rate optimization lowers the price per unit (commitments, negotiated pricing, licensing); usage optimization lowers the units consumed (rightsizing, scheduling, removing idle resources). Usage work should usually come first, so that you do not commit to waste.
Utilization asks how much of the committed capacity or spend was actually used; coverage asks how much of the usage commitments covered. High coverage with low utilization signals over-commitment.

Usage-based commitments (reservations) lock in a resource type, size or region for deeper discounts. Spend-based commitments (savings plans) commit an hourly amount that applies across eligible usage, with a breadth that ranges from one instance family (AWS EC2 Instance Savings Plans) to many services and regions.

A capacity reservation guarantees that capacity will be available but gives no discount. A reservation or Reserved Instance gives a discount but does not guarantee capacity unless it is zonal; the two are often combined.
A negotiated commitment is a contract-level promise of total spend that earns organisation-wide discounts or credits. A savings plan is a self-service hourly commitment that discounts eligible usage.

The headline discount is the advertised reduction on covered usage. The effective savings rate is what was actually saved across all eligible spend after unused commitments, and it is the honest measure of a commitment programme.

Billed cost shows charges when they are invoiced, so an upfront commitment makes one month spike. Amortized (effective) cost spreads that purchase across the usage it discounts, and it is the view allocation and unit economics should use.
List cost prices usage at public rates. Contracted cost prices it at negotiated rates before commitment discounts, so the difference between them measures the value of the negotiated agreement.
A budget is an approved limit that you plan to stay within. A forecast is a projection of what you will actually spend, and comparing the two shows variance early.
Cost savings lower spend against the current baseline and show up on the bill. Cost avoidance prevents spend that would have occurred, which is real value but never appears as a bill reduction.

TBM allocates all IT costs, including staff, data centres and licences, through a standard taxonomy for strategic IT finance. FinOps focuses on variable, usage-based technology spend and on near-real-time collaboration with engineers.
TCO adds up what an option costs over its life. ROI relates the benefits to those costs, so an option can have the lowest TCO and still the worst ROI.
ROI is a ratio that ignores when cash flows occur. NPV discounts each cash flow to today, so it favours earlier benefits and shows absolute value created.
Payback tells you how quickly the investment is recovered but ignores the time value of money and benefits after payback. NPV accounts for both.

BYOL reuses licences you already own and pays only for infrastructure, but you must follow licence-mobility rules. Licence-included pricing bundles the licence into the hourly rate, which is simpler and more elastic but often dearer at steady state.

pairs.difference: A FinOps Scope is a business-aligned segment of technology spend to which FinOps practices are applied. An Azure scope is a level in the resource hierarchy at which RBAC, Azure Policy, budgets and cost views apply. Same word, different concept.
A KPI tracks progress towards a business or practice objective, such as cost per order. An SLO is an internal reliability target for a service, such as 99.9% successful requests, measured by SLIs.
